summary: Documents IANA assignments for GMPLS RSVP-TE usage and extensions related to the Automatically Switched Optical Network architecture from the ITU-T. It focuses on the signaling aspects of the GMPLS suite for requesting circuits such as SONET/SDH and optical transport connections.

plainLanguage.summary: Optical network gear from different groups needs matching number codes. This note writes down which codes were assigned for the optical signaling so everyone is on the same page.

how does call connection separation work in ason
subtitle: GMPLS signaling extensions for automatic switched optical networks.

tldr.problem: Automatic Switched Optical Networks (ASON) from the ITU-T require capabilities that the basic GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling protocol did not provide, such as call and connection separation, soft permanent connections, and robust control plane failure handling.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3474 documents extensions to GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling messages and objects, including a new Call Identifier object to separate calls from connections, soft permanent connection labels, and mechanisms for label association in multi-hop optical paths.
tldr.outcome: These extensions enable GMPLS-based control of optical networks that comply with ITU-T ASON standards, allowing dynamic circuit provisioning in optical transport networks.

today: RFC 3474 is an Informational document that documented GMPLS extensions required for ITU-T ASON networks. While GMPLS has continued to evolve, these ASON-specific extensions remain important for carriers operating optical networks that need to comply with international standards for multi-vendor circuit provisioning.

sections.title: Introduction and ASON Requirements
sections.content:
The Generalized MultiProtocol Label Switching (GMPLS) suite provides protocol support for requesting circuits in networks using different technologies, including Synchronous Optical NETwork/Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SONET/SDH) and Optical Transport Networks (OTNs). The ITU-T's Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) architecture defines how carriers' optical networks should allow dynamic circuit provisioning.

This document extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling to meet ASON requirements that the base GMPLS specification did not address, including support for soft permanent connections, call and connection separation, control plane restart capabilities, label scoping issues in multi-hop paths, and User-to-Network Interface (UNI) and External Network-to-Network Interface (E-NNI) signaling sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS is a protocol for controlling optical equipment. This document adds new features to GMPLS so it can work with the international ASON standard for how optical networks should operate.

sections.title: Soft Permanent Connections and Call Separation
sections.content:
Soft permanent connections (SPC) are pre-provisioned circuits that blend aspects of permanent and switched connections. This document defines a new SPC_LABEL sub-object within GENERALIZED_UNI to identify the permanent ingress segment of such connections, helping align GMPLS terminology with the ASON model.

Call and connection separation is fundamental to ASON: a call (a high-level service request) may have one or more associated connections (the actual data paths). GMPLS originally treated these as a single entity. This RFC introduces a CALL_ID object that carries a globally unique call identifier across signaling messages, allowing network elements to distinguish between call-level operations and connection-level operations.
sections.plainLanguage: A 'call' is like asking for a phone line; a 'connection' is the actual wires used. The system needs to tell the difference between managing the request and managing the actual circuit.

sections.title: RSVP-TE Message Extensions
sections.content:
GMPLS signaling uses RSVP-TE messages (Path, Resv, PathTear, PathErr, and Notify) to request and manage connections. This RFC mandates that for ASON-compliant networks, the CALL_ID object MUST be included in Path, Resv, PathTear, PathErr, and Notify messages. The Path message also MUST include a GENERALIZED_UNI object for ASON networks.

Processing rules specify that the CALL_ID object is forwarded unmodified through the network from ingress to egress, allowing all intermediate nodes to recognize and route based on the call identifier. The CALL_ID carries either an operator-specific identifier (for single-domain calls) or a globally unique identifier (including country code, carrier code, and unique access point code) for inter-domain calls.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages asking for circuits now include a special field that says which call the circuit belongs to, so all the network equipment knows the full context.

sections.title: Control Plane Failure Recovery and Label Scoping
sections.content:
Optical networks require robust handling of control plane failures (when the signaling network is disrupted). This RFC leverages GMPLS restart mechanisms but adds guidance that control plane nodes SHOULD persistently store call and connection state. If a control element fails, it can recover local state from storage rather than relying solely on neighboring nodes to re-synchronize it.

A critical challenge in multi-hop optical networks is that label values are locally significant. A timeslot or wavelength label received from an upstream neighbor may not directly correspond to the same resource at the local node, especially when non-GMPLS-capable switching elements are traversed. This RFC clarifies that label association must be handled through manual provisioning or dynamic discovery, ensuring correct mappings across domains.
sections.plainLanguage: If a network device fails and restarts, it remembers the circuits it was managing. Also, labels (the names for circuits) change as they cross different equipment, so the system needs to know how to translate them.

sections.title: UNI and E-NNI Signaling Sessions
sections.content:
ASON defines different signaling interfaces: the User-to-Network Interface (UNI, where users request circuits from the network) and the External Network-to-Network Interface (E-NNI, where different carriers' networks coordinate circuit provisioning). This RFC extends the RSVP-TE SESSION object with new C-Types to explicitly identify message types: UNI IPv4, UNI IPv6, E-NNI IPv4, and E-NNI IPv6 sessions.

These extensions allow a single physical interface to support multiple types of signaling requests and enable networks to route signaling messages correctly based on the interface type. The destination address in the SESSION object identifies the downstream controller for message routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks have different kinds of signaling conversations: customers asking for circuits, and carriers talking to each other. The system needs to tag messages so everyone knows which kind of conversation is happening.

sections.title: Error Handling and Additional Error Cases
sections.content:
RFC 3474 defines additional error codes and values to support the new ASON capabilities, allowing network elements to report failure conditions specific to call/connection separation, soft permanent connections, and inter-carrier signaling issues. These error cases help implementers diagnose problems in multi-vendor optical networks.

The RFC relies on underlying GMPLS security mechanisms and the security services provided by lower-layer protocols such as IPsec or TLS, rather than adding security features directly to the ASON extensions themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong with a call or connection, the system reports a specific error code so the network operator knows what happened.
